section.title: Clean and Unclean, and the Syrophoenician Woman
section.sectionRationale: Jesus confronts the Pharisees over their tradition, exposing how human rules had nullified God's command and locating true defilement in the heart, not in unwashed hands or foods. Mark then shows the gospel crossing the boundary: a Gentile woman's persistent faith wins her daughter's deliverance, and a deaf and mute man in Gentile territory is healed. What defiles and what cleanses are redefined, and the door opens to the nations.
section.thesis: Defilement is not a matter of hands or foods but of the sinful heart, so Jesus declares all foods clean and overturns tradition that voids God's word; and the same Lord, freeing a Gentile girl and opening deaf ears, shows that His cleansing mercy reaches beyond Israel to the nations.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the clash over the tradition of the elders; the teaching on what truly defiles; and two mercies in Gentile lands, the Syrophoenician woman and the deaf-mute man.

units.label: The tradition of the elders
units.note: you nullify the word of God by your tradition

verses.text: Then the Pharisees and some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem gathered around Jesus,
and they saw some of His disciples eating with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed.
Now in holding to the tradition of the elders, the Pharisees and all the Jews do not eat until they wash their hands ceremonially.
And on returning from the market, they do not eat unless they wash. And there are many other traditions for them to observe, including the washing of cups, pitchers, kettles, and couches for dining.
So the Pharisees and scribes questioned Jesus: “Why do Your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders? Instead, they eat with defiled hands.”
Jesus answered them, “Isaiah prophesied correctly about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.
They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.’
You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the {{paradosis|tradition}} of men.”
He went on to say, “You neatly set aside the command of God to maintain your own tradition.
For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’ and ‘Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death.’
But you say that if a man says to his father or mother, ‘Whatever you would have received from me is {{korban|Corban}}’ (that is, a gift devoted to God),
he is no longer permitted to do anything for his father or mother.
Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down. And you do so in many such matters.”

units.label: What truly defiles
units.note: from within, out of the heart

verses.text: Once again Jesus called the crowd to Him and said, “All of you, listen to Me and understand:
Nothing that enters a man from the outside can {{koinoo|defile}} him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.”
After Jesus had left the crowd and gone into the house, His disciples inquired about the parable.
“Are you still so dull?” He asked. “Do you not understand? Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him,
because it does not enter his heart, but it goes into the stomach and then is eliminated.” (Thus all foods are clean.)
He continued: “What comes out of a man, that is what defiles him.
For from within the hearts of men come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery,
greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness.
All these evils come from within, and these are what defile a man.”

units.label: The faith of the Syrophoenician woman
units.note: even the dogs eat the children's crumbs

verses.text: Jesus left that place and went to the region of Tyre. Not wanting anyone to know He was there, He entered a house, but was unable to escape their notice.
Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit soon heard about Jesus, and she came and fell at His feet.
Now she was a Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin, and she kept asking Jesus to drive the demon out of her daughter.
“First let the children have their fill,” He said. “For it is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.”
“Yes, Lord,” she replied, “even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.”
Then Jesus told her, “Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter.”
And she went home and found her child lying on the bed, and the demon was gone.
Then Jesus left the region of Tyre and went through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee and into the region of the Decapolis.
Some people brought to Him a man who was deaf and hardly able to speak, and they begged Jesus to place His hand on him.
So Jesus took him aside privately, away from the crowd, and put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue.
And looking up to heaven, He sighed deeply and said to him, “{{ephphatha|Ephphatha}}!” (which means, “Be opened!”).
Immediately the man’s ears were opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak plainly.
Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone. But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it.
The people were utterly astonished and said, “He has done all things well! He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!”

paradosis.gloss: A tradition, something handed down. The tradition of the elders was the growing body of human rules meant to guard the law. Jesus condemns not tradition as such but tradition that displaces and even nullifies the commandment of God, honouring human precepts over the divine word.

korban.gloss: Corban, an offering devoted to God. By vowing property as Corban, a person could technically withhold support from aging parents while appearing pious. Jesus exposes this as a way of using religious ritual to evade the plain command to honour father and mother.

koinoo.gloss: To make common or unclean, to defile. Jesus overturns the assumption that defilement comes from without, from foods or unwashed hands. What truly defiles a person is what comes out of the heart; sin, not diet, makes one unclean before God.

ephphatha.gloss: Be opened, the Aramaic word Jesus spoke to the deaf man, preserved by Mark and translated for his readers. The command that opens deaf ears and looses a bound tongue enacts the prophetic hope of Isaiah 35, a sign that the day of salvation has dawned.

basic.context: The Pharisees criticize Jesus' disciples for eating without the ceremonial handwashing their tradition required. Jesus turns the charge back on them: they honour God with their lips while their hearts are far from Him, and their traditions actually cancel God's commands, as when a man declares his money Corban, dedicated to God, and so refuses to help his own parents. Then Jesus teaches that food does not defile a person; defilement comes from within, from the sinful heart. Mark adds two scenes in Gentile territory: a Syrophoenician woman whose witty, humble faith wins her daughter's deliverance, and a deaf man with a speech impediment whom Jesus heals with the word Ephphatha, be opened.
basic.hermeneutics: The theme is what makes a person clean or unclean before God. Jesus relocates the problem from the outside to the heart, and Mark notes that this declares all foods clean, a landmark for the gospel's later welcome of Gentiles. The two Gentile miracles that follow are not incidental; they show the cleansing mercy of Jesus reaching the nations, precisely those the food laws had kept at a distance.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus attacks the paradosis, tradition, that nullifies God's command, exposing the abuse of korban, Corban, a gift devoted to God used to dodge caring for parents. Nothing outside can koinoo, defile, a person; sin from the heart does. And to the deaf man He says ephphatha, be opened.
basic.typology: The opening of deaf ears and a bound tongue fulfils Isaiah 35, the sign of the coming age of salvation. The declaration that all foods are clean anticipates the tearing down of the wall between Jew and Gentile accomplished in Christ. The heart that defiles points to the need for a new heart God promised.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Lord who reads the heart, who has authority to declare all foods clean, and who fulfils the prophecies of the age of salvation by opening ears and loosing tongues. He extends His cleansing mercy to a Gentile woman and a Gentile man.
basic.god: God desires hearts, not mere ritual, and He is grieved when human tradition buries His word. God's mercy is not confined to Israel; He hears the cry of a Gentile mother and opens the ears of a Gentile man.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 29 is quoted against empty worship. Isaiah 35 promises deaf ears opened. Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 promise a new heart, the answer to the heart that defiles.
basic.oneStory: The problem the whole Bible traces is the human heart, and here Jesus names it: defilement flows from within. He redefines clean and unclean, opens the way to the nations, and enacts the promised age of salvation by opening deaf ears. The story is moving toward the cross, where the unclean heart is cleansed and the wall between Jew and Gentile comes down.

context.literary:
Chapter 7 is built around a single word, defiled, and then moves from a question about hands to a question about hearts and finally to two bodies. The first unit, verses 1 to 13, is an argument with Jerusalem scribes. The second, verses 14 to 23, is a public saying followed by a private explanation, a pattern Mark uses for parables, Mark 4:10-12. Notice that the disciples are rebuked for being dull, verse 18, exactly as they were at the end of chapter 6. The third and fourth units, verses 24 to 37, are two miracles in Gentile country. Reading the four as one movement shows how Mark thinks. A ruling about food becomes a story about a Gentile woman at a table, and her answer about crumbs reaches back to the argument about bread.

Mark's own comments are an important feature of the chapter. He pauses to explain Jewish custom to his readers, verses 3 and 4, translates Corban, verse 11, and adds a parenthesis in verse 19, thus all foods are clean. The explanations show that he is writing for a mixed audience, and that he wants Gentile believers to understand why a food dispute mattered. The numbered list of vices in verses 21 and 22 is a deliberate counterweight to the lists of foods in Leviticus 11: where the law lists what may and may not go into the mouth, Jesus lists what comes out of the heart.

Verse 16 is missing in the BSB as in many early manuscripts, and the chapter moves from verse 15 to verse 17 without it. Nothing hangs on this, since the saying of verse 15 is repeated in verses 18 to 23.

The final verse is deliberately large. The crowd's verdict, he has done all things well, verse 37, echoes the way the creation account ends, when God looked at all He had made and found it very good, Genesis 1:31. Mark closes a chapter about uncleanness with an echo of creation, as though Jesus were beginning to make all things good again.
context.historical:
The scribes came from Jerusalem, which in Mark is an ominous detail. Mark 3:22 had already shown scribes from Jerusalem accusing Jesus of working by Beelzebul. They represent the centre of religious authority sent north to examine the new teacher. The tradition they defend was an oral body of teaching that grew up to build a fence around the written law. In the law, ritual washing before eating was required of priests as they came to minister, Exodus 30:20. The Pharisees had extended the priestly standard to every pious Israelite at ordinary meals, so that the table at home was treated like the altar. The rules were later written down in the Mishnah, which has a section on vows and another on the washing of hands, but in Jesus' day they were a living tradition passed on by teachers.

Mark mentions the washing of cups, pitchers and kettles. Purity in this system was not a matter of hygiene but of avoiding contact with anything that might carry ritual contamination, and the marketplace, where one might have touched Gentiles or unclean goods, was a particular risk. The stakes were identity. Food laws and purity rules were among the things that set Israel apart, and under Greek and Roman pressure many Jews had died rather than eat what was forbidden. To loosen those habits was, for these men, to loosen Israel itself.

The Corban rule, verses 11 and 12, is a legal evasion that is attested in the way Jesus describes it. A man could declare his goods as dedicated to God and so make them unavailable to anyone else, parents included, while still keeping them for his own use. It satisfied a vow in form and cancelled the fifth commandment in effect. The commandment in Exodus 20:12 and the penalty for cursing a parent in Exodus 21:17 show how seriously the law took the matter.

The Gentile scenes are set in Tyre, a Phoenician port on the Mediterranean, and the Decapolis, ten largely Gentile cities east of the lake. Tyre had long depended on Galilee for food, as Acts 12:20 states for a later time, and it is often suggested that the woman's reply about crumbs reflects that relationship. She is called a Greek, which in Mark means a Gentile of Greek culture, and a Syrophoenician by origin, a term that distinguished Phoenicians in Syria from those in North Africa.
context.canonical:
The confrontation takes up the prophets' complaint against religion without a heart. Mark quotes Isaiah 29:13, in which people honour God with their lips while their hearts are far from Him. The prophets said the same elsewhere: God desires mercy, not sacrifice, Hosea 6:6, and the law that matters is written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33. Ezekiel 36:25-27 promises that God Himself will sprinkle clean water, remove the heart of stone and give a new heart and a new spirit. The saying in verse 15 is not a new idea in Israel. It presses the old promise to a point where it can no longer be avoided: if defilement comes from the heart, then only a new heart can cleanse it.

On food, the Old Testament sets a long story. All living things were given as food after the flood, Genesis 9:3. The distinctions of Leviticus 11 were then set for Israel as a holy people. Mark's comment, thus all foods are clean, implies that the restriction has run its course. The New Testament shows that the church needed time to absorb this. Peter's vision in Acts 10:14-15 required three repetitions before he accepted that he should not call anything unclean that God had made clean, and the council in Acts 15:19-20 had to decide what to ask of Gentile believers. Later Peter wavered at Antioch, Galatians 2:12. Paul concluded that nothing is unclean in itself, Romans 14:14, that everything God created is good and should be received with thanks, 1 Timothy 4:4-5, and that rules such as do not touch, do not taste have no value against the flesh, Colossians 2:20-23.

The Gentile section continues a thread too. Elijah was sent to a widow of Zarephath in Sidon, 1 Kings 17:9, and Jesus later cites that, Luke 4:25-26. Isaiah promised that foreigners would be brought to God's holy mountain and that His house would be a house of prayer for all nations, Isaiah 56:6-7. Isaiah 35:5-6 promised opened ears and a tongue that shouts for joy, and the crowd's reaction in verse 37 recognises that promise. Paul later says Christ became a servant to the circumcised so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy, Romans 15:8-9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wrote this chapter so that Gentile believers in particular would understand why they were welcome without keeping the food laws, and so that Jewish believers would see that the welcome did not come from Jesus ignoring the law but from His reading its purpose. The key move is to show that Jesus does not attack Scripture. He quotes Isaiah and Moses against the scribes and accuses them of being the ones who set Scripture aside. The target is a religion that treats human rules as God's word.

He also wanted readers to feel what the heart list in verses 21 and 22 costs. It begins with thoughts and ends with foolishness, and in between it moves through sins of the body, the hand, the tongue and the eye. No one reads it without finding themselves on the list. That is the point. The problem is universal, and no washing reaches it.

The two miracles show the answer. A mother who has been told she has no claim is given what she did not deserve, and a man who cannot hear is unmade and remade by a word. Mark wants readers to see that the one who declares food clean is also the one who can make a person clean, and that He does not stop at the border of Israel.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The scribes' practices are described, not endorsed, and Jesus' response is not a general rule against all tradition. He does not condemn washing, and Mark does not say the disciples were right to skip it out of principle. He condemns the habit of treating a man-made rule as equal to God's word, and especially when the rule cancels a commandment such as honouring parents. Application today means testing every custom by whether it serves or replaces the word of God.

The saying that nothing from outside defiles was lived out slowly, as the book of Acts shows. Believers should not treat it as permission for carelessness about the body or about conscience. Paul, who agreed that nothing is unclean in itself, still tells believers not to wound a weaker conscience over food, Romans 14:20-21.

The Syrophoenician woman's story is also not a template for bargaining with Jesus, as though persistence earns a miracle. It is a record of how one person's humility and faith met His mercy, and a preview of Gentile inclusion. The command that follows from it is not to out-argue Jesus but to come to Him with need and trust. Finally, the healing of the deaf man is something Jesus did, with His own methods, and nothing here prescribes touch, spittle or a particular word as a technique for believers.

debates.question: Why does Jesus first seem to refuse the Syrophoenician woman with the words about dogs?

views.label: A test that draws out and honours her faith
views.case: Jesus states the God-ordained order, to the Jew first, using a household image; His words invite rather than dismiss, and He praises the humble, persistent faith her clever reply reveals, granting her request.

views.label: An enacted lesson on the widening mission
views.case: The scene dramatizes for the disciples that the children's bread will indeed reach the nations; even now the crumbs fall from the table, and the Gentile mother receives the very mercy the food laws had fenced off.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree Jesus is not harsh or reluctant but is drawing out and commending a faith that becomes a preview of the Gentile welcome the gospel will bring.

debates.question: Does Jesus abolish the Old Testament food laws?

views.label: He fulfils and transcends them, revealing their deeper point
views.case: By declaring all foods clean, Jesus shows that the laws pointed to a deeper holiness of heart; with His coming, the ceremonial distinctions that separated Israel from the nations have served their purpose and give way.

views.label: He exposes their misuse while affirming the moral law
views.case: Jesus targets a religion of external ritual that ignored the heart and even nullified moral commands like honouring parents; the enduring demand is inward purity, which the food laws could never produce.

debates.bearing: Both hold that the point is the heart: outward observance was never the true measure of cleanness, and in Christ the barrier the food laws erected between Jew and Gentile is coming down.

study.originalLanguages:
The root of the dispute is a word that is easy to pass over. In verse 2 the disciples eat with koinais hands, which Mark glosses as unwashed. The word koinos means common, shared by all, and in Jewish usage it came to mean ritually common, not set apart as holy. It is the word Peter uses in Acts 10:14 when he says he has never eaten anything koinon or akatharton, common or unclean. Jesus uses the verb of the same family in verse 15, koinoun, to make common. His point is that what defiles is not something that touches a person from outside but something that originates in the heart.

The heart, kardia, is in Hebrew thought the whole inner person, mind, will and affections, not just feelings. When Jesus says the evil things come from within the kardia, verse 21, He is speaking the language of Jeremiah 17:9, where the heart is deceitful above all things. The vice list has thirteen items, and the two nearest the end, in verse 22, are worth noticing. One is literally the evil eye, which the BSB renders envy, an idiom for a grudging, covetous look. The last is aphrosyne, foolishness, which in Scripture is moral as much as intellectual, as in Luke 12:20. The list ends with the fool, who says there is no God, a hint that the root problem is practical atheism of the heart.

The Corban dispute rests on a Hebrew word. Qorban in the law means an offering brought near to God, as in Leviticus 1:2. Mark translates it as a gift devoted to God. Jesus' charge is that a word meant to express devotion is being used as a legal device to avoid duty. The word for annul in verse 13, akyroo, means to make void, to deprive of authority, and is the verb used in Galatians 3:17 of a law that cannot cancel a covenant. The scribes, who claimed to protect the law, were making it void.

Verse 19 ends with a short comment that is grammatically awkward. The Greek participle is masculine and agrees with the subject of the preceding sentence, which is Jesus. Most translations therefore take it as Mark's comment on what Jesus was doing, declaring all foods clean, as the BSB parenthesis does.

In the woman's scene the word for dogs in verses 27 and 28 is a diminutive, kynaria, which means little dogs or house dogs. The diminutive softens the image, since these are pets under the table and not street dogs, and it allows her to take the picture and turn it. The word for the crumbs of the children, psichion, refers to small scraps. She accepts the order of the table, children first, and asks only for what is already falling. Her address, Lord, kyrie, is more than courtesy.

The deaf man is described by a rare word, mogilalos, verse 32, which is translated as hardly able to speak. It appears in the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 35:6, where the tongue of the mogilalos will shout for joy. The word is not used again in the New Testament, which makes the allusion unusually clear. Jesus' command, ephphatha, is Aramaic, and Mark preserves it with a translation, as he does in Mark 5:41. The healing is described as the loosing of a bond of the tongue, and the man spoke plainly, a word meaning rightly or correctly.

typology.type: The new heart promised through Ezekiel and Jeremiah
typology.fulfillment: Jesus locates defilement in the heart, and the prophets had already promised a cure at that level. God would sprinkle clean water, remove the heart of stone and give a new heart and spirit, Ezekiel 36:25-27, and write His law on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33. The old washings dealt with the outside, and Jesus' diagnosis shows why they could never be enough. In Christ the promise is carried out by His Spirit, so that Paul can write that believers are washed, sanctified and justified, 1 Corinthians 6:11. The type falls short only in that the washing of the old covenant could not change anyone's heart, so the cleansing in Christ is not an improved version of the same thing but a different kind.

typology.type: Food laws as a dividing wall
typology.fulfillment: The clean and unclean distinctions of Leviticus 11 kept Israel separate from the nations, and they marked a fence around holiness. Mark's comment that all foods are clean removes the fence at the level of the table. Paul says Christ tore down the dividing wall of hostility and made the two one, Ephesians 2:14-15. The escalation is from a boundary that kept Gentiles at a distance to a table where Jews and Gentiles eat together, which is what Peter learned at Cornelius's house, Acts 10:28. The type is not undone in its purpose, which was holiness, but in its form: holiness now means a cleansed heart, not a restricted menu.

typology.type: A Gentile woman at the table
typology.fulfillment: Elijah was sent to a Gentile widow in Sidon during a famine, 1 Kings 17:9, a sign that God's provision was never meant for Israel alone, as Jesus says in Luke 4:25-26. Here Jesus is in the same region, and a Gentile mother receives bread for her child. The escalation is that the prophet's visit becomes a pattern for the church. Paul says Christ confirmed the promises to the patriarchs so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy, Romans 15:8-9. The type falls short in that Elijah's widow was fed, while the woman here asks for and receives a rescue from an unclean spirit, and Jesus does it from a distance by His word.

typology.type: Ears opened and tongues loosed, Isaiah 35
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah pictured the coming salvation as a time when the eyes of the blind would be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped and the mute tongue would shout for joy, Isaiah 35:5-6. The word Mark uses for the man's speech problem is the very word Isaiah's Greek uses for the tongue that shouts. Jesus, in the region of the Decapolis, does this in the presence of Gentiles. The correspondence is exact, and the escalation is that the age of salvation has arrived in a person. The type is partly fulfilled only: the man will hear and speak again, but he will still die, and the full removal of every disability waits for the new creation.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first through His authority over the law's categories. Only God has the standing to redraw the lines He drew. Mark's comment in verse 19 shows what the teaching amounted to, and the disciples will need years and a vision of Peter's to understand it. For a Jewish reader of that time, a man who said that food does not defile was either a blasphemer or the Lord of the law. Mark leaves no doubt which. Jesus quotes Isaiah as one who knows the prophet's real meaning and speaks with the authority of one who stands above the commandments of men.

Second, the chapter leads to Christ as the answer to the heart problem He diagnoses. A teacher who only named the list of verses 21 and 22 would leave his hearers condemned. But Jesus does not end with the diagnosis. In the chapters that follow He gives a path through the cross, and the New Testament says what He accomplished there. He cleanses what the law's washings could not, Hebrews 9:13-14. The blood of Christ cleanses the conscience from dead works to serve the living God. The Jesus who points to the dirty heart is the Jesus who goes to the cross to make it clean.

Third, He is the one who is touched by need. In Tyre the woman falls at His feet and persists, and Jesus, who has just taught that nothing from outside defiles, is not made unclean by a Gentile's request. The same holds in the next scene, where He puts His fingers in the ears of a deaf man and touches his tongue. Mark has already shown Him touching a leper, Mark 1:41, and being touched by a woman with a flow of blood, Mark 5:30. Each time the uncleanness does not pass to Him; the cleanness passes to them. That is the logic of the incarnation, which Isaiah expressed when he wrote that by His wounds we are healed, Isaiah 53:5.

Fourth, the woman's answer reveals Him as one who delights to be overcome by faith. His words about the children's bread name the order of salvation, to the Jew first, which Paul affirms in Romans 1:16. Her answer does not reject that order but asks for a share inside it. Jesus says, because of this answer, the demon has left. There is a hint of Christ delighting to be taken at His own word.

Fifth, the crowd's cry, He has done all things well, belongs to Him. The man who is called from deafness by a word is a small version of the new creation, and the sighing in verse 34 shows that He feels the weight of what He is undoing, as He will in Gethsemane. He is not a distant healer. He looks to heaven, groans and speaks the word that opens.

A caution is in order. The spit and the fingers are not a spell, and the details are not coded allegories. What the text stresses is the word and the touch of the one who has authority over cleanness and sickness.
study.god:
This passage presents God as one who looks at the heart. Samuel was told that people look at the outward appearance but the LORD looks at the heart, 1 Samuel 16:7, and Jesus does the same here. God's concern throughout Scripture is not the absence of ritual but the presence of devotion, and the Isaiah quotation in verses 6 and 7 shows that He is grieved by worship that is only lips. The God of this chapter cannot be satisfied with a clean exterior, and He is not fooled by one.

He is the God of the word, and He takes His own word seriously. Jesus charges the scribes with annulling the word of God by their tradition, and the commandment He chooses to defend is the fifth, honour your father and mother. The God who gave the commandments also gave a penalty for dishonouring parents, and Jesus will not allow clever religion to cancel either. Holiness in this chapter is not distinct from ordinary duties like caring for aged parents. It is carried out in them.

He is also the God who made all things good. Mark's comment that all foods are clean agrees with the verdict of Genesis 1:31 and the permission of Genesis 9:3. The food laws were a gift for a season, to teach Israel what holiness looks like, and they now have done their work. The doctrine of creation and the doctrine of redemption agree: what God made is good, and what is wrong is in the human heart.

He is a God of mercy that crosses boundaries. A Gentile mother in Tyre and a Gentile man in the Decapolis meet Him, and He gives them what they ask. The choice of Israel was never meant as the exclusion of the nations, a point the Old Testament had made in Isaiah 56:6-7 and Psalm 67, and which Paul states in Romans 15:8-9. God's particular choice has a universal purpose.

He is a God who is moved. Jesus sighs deeply, verse 34, as He looks up to heaven. The sigh is not a sign of weakness; it is a sign that God is not indifferent to the suffering of a deaf man. Romans 8:26 says the Spirit Himself groans for us, and the sigh in Mark is the Son's share in that.

For worship, the chapter calls for honesty. We are told to draw near, and not only with our lips. The prayer that fits it is the psalmist's, create in me a clean heart, O God, Psalm 51:10, which asks for the thing no washing can supply. It also calls for open doors in the gathered life of the church. If God's mercy reaches the foreigner at the table, His people cannot be content to leave the foreigner outside.

crossReferences.note: God complains that the people honour Him with their lips while their hearts are far away and their worship is rules taught by men. Mark quotes the verse in the Greek translation. Jesus applies it as a description of the scribes, which shows that He reads Isaiah's rebuke as an enduring warning, not only a judgment on a past generation.

The fifth commandment, honour your father and your mother, is the commandment the Corban rule undermined. Jesus pairs it with Exodus 21:17, the penalty for cursing a parent, to show that the law treated the matter as grave. The passage proves that Jesus defended the moral law even as He loosened ceremonial law.

This is the start of the food laws, the clean and unclean animals God set before Israel. Mark's statement that all foods are clean refers to this system. The laws were given to teach a people to distinguish the holy from the common, and the Gospel reads that lesson as having been fulfilled in the cleansing of the heart.

The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. The saying matches Jesus' list of evils from within. Jeremiah asked who can understand the heart and also promised that God would one day write His law there, Jeremiah 31:33. The diagnosis and the cure both come from the prophets.

God promises to sprinkle clean water, remove the heart of stone and put a new spirit inside His people. These are the verses that answer the problem of verses 21 to 23. The cleansing Jesus' hearers needed was not on the hands or the cups but at the centre, and God had promised to supply it.

Peter protests that he has never eaten anything impure or unclean, and a voice tells him not to call anything impure that God has made clean. The vision shows how slowly even an apostle absorbed what Jesus taught in Mark 7. It also shows that the saying was understood as reaching beyond food to people, as Acts 10:28 makes clear.

Paul says he is convinced in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself. This is the apostolic statement of Mark 7:15, applied to a church where some still held scruples. Paul adds that for someone who regards a thing as unclean it is unclean, so that love must guide how the freedom is used.

Paul asks why believers who have died with Christ submit to rules like do not handle, do not taste, do not touch. He says such rules are based on human commands, appear wise and have no value against the indulgence of the flesh. The passage matches Jesus' charge that the tradition of the elders was human precepts.

God sends Elijah to a widow in Sidon during a famine. Jesus later points to the episode when He says that God's help was not limited to Israel, Luke 4:25-26. The woman of Tyre stands in this line, a Gentile mother whose need meets the mercy of God's prophet and then of God's Son.

The eyes of the blind will be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped and the mute tongue will shout for joy. The healing of the deaf man with a speech difficulty matches the promise closely, down to the rare word for the speech problem. The crowd's wonder in verse 37 recognises the promised age.

Christ has torn down the dividing wall of hostility and abolished in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees, to make one new man out of the two. The declaration of Mark 7:19 begins the process Paul describes, and the food laws were part of the wall.

God says He desires mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. Jesus quotes the same text elsewhere, Matthew 9:13, and the whole chapter works on it. The Corban rule shows religion that keeps offerings and loses mercy, and the woman's story shows mercy winning.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a world that God called very good and with a people who were meant to live in His presence without shame. After the fall the problem is not the creation, which stays good, but the heart, and the long middle of the story is about how God might deal with it. The law is given to a people who were to be distinct, and the food rules and washings are one means of teaching Israel that holiness is real and costly. They cannot go further than that. The prophets say as much. They complain that the people's hearts are far away and promise that God Himself will one day give a new heart.

Mark 7 sits at the point where that promise is beginning to be kept. Jesus names the human problem with the exact precision of the prophets, from within, out of the heart. He then declares that the signs and fences that taught Israel about holiness have done their work. The result is the beginning of a people no longer defined by its menu. The Gentile woman and the deaf man in the following scenes are the first fruits of that people, the outsiders who now have a place at the table.

What the chapter sets up is the church of Jews and Gentiles together. Acts will spend chapters on how that happens, through Peter's vision and the council at Jerusalem, and Paul's letters will carry the argument to Romans, Galatians and Ephesians. The enemy of the church's unity is not the absence of rules but the presence of the same heart problem Jesus names, which is why the cross is the only answer. At the cross the dividing wall comes down and the heart can be washed, Hebrews 10:22.

The story ends in a city whose gates are never shut and where nothing unclean will ever enter, Revelation 21:27, because the people who live there have been made clean. The nations bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:26. Every part of the chapter is heard again there. The Gentile woman's crumbs become a place at the wedding supper, Revelation 19:9, and the tongue that was bound shouts for joy in the new creation, as Isaiah 35 promised.

quiz.q: What was Jesus' main charge against the Pharisees' tradition?

options.text: They elevated human tradition so highly that it nullified the commandment of God.
options.note: Mark 7:8-13; their tradition, like the Corban abuse, set aside God's clear commands.

options.text: They added extra washings that were merely unnecessary.
options.note: The washings were part of it, but the deeper charge was that tradition voided God's word.

options.text: They failed to keep their own traditions carefully enough.
options.note: The problem was not laxity toward tradition but exalting tradition over God's command.

options.text: They followed the written law of Moses too strictly.
options.note: Jesus upheld Moses; He condemned human tradition that overrode Moses, as with honouring parents.

quiz.q: According to Jesus, what truly defiles a person?

options.text: The evil that comes out of the heart, such as sinful thoughts and deeds, not what enters from outside.
options.note: Mark 7:20-23 locates defilement in the heart, listing sins that flow from within.

options.text: Eating certain foods or failing to wash properly.
options.note: The opposite of Jesus' point; He says food does not defile and declares all foods clean.

options.text: Both unclean food and an unclean heart together.
options.note: Jesus specifically denies that food defiles; He locates defilement in the heart alone.

options.text: Contact with Gentiles and sinners.
options.note: Jesus reaches Gentiles with mercy; defilement is from the heart, not from such contact.

quiz.q: What does Mark's comment, thus all foods are clean, signal?

options.text: A turning point removing the food-law barrier, opening the way to full fellowship with Gentiles.
options.note: The declaration prepares for Acts 10 and the gospel's welcome of the nations.

options.text: That believers may now eat whatever they like.
options.note: True practically, but the deeper significance is the falling of the barrier between Jew and Gentile.

options.text: That the Old Testament food laws were always pointless.
options.note: The laws had a real purpose that pointed beyond themselves; they were not pointless but are now fulfilled.

options.text: That the moral law no longer applies either.
options.note: Jesus intensifies the moral demand of the heart; only the ceremonial food distinction is set aside.

quiz.q: How did the Syrophoenician woman respond to Jesus' words about the children's bread?

options.text: With humble, persistent faith, saying even the dogs eat the children's crumbs, and Jesus granted her request.
options.note: Mark 7:28-29; her faith-filled reply won her daughter's deliverance.

options.text: She accepted His words and quietly went away without her request.
options.note: She did not give up; she pressed her case with faith and received the miracle.

options.text: She persisted in asking and trusted Jesus despite the hard-sounding words.
options.note: True that she persisted, but the fuller answer names her humble, witty faith and the granted request.

options.text: She argued that she deserved the same status as Israel.
options.note: She claimed no equal status; she humbly asked only for crumbs of mercy.

quiz.q: What does the healing of the deaf and mute man reveal?

options.text: That Jesus fulfils the prophetic promise of the age of salvation, opening deaf ears and loosing bound tongues.
options.note: The miracle echoes Isaiah 35:5-6; the crowd marvels that He does all things well.

options.text: That Jesus could heal physical ailments.
options.note: True, but the deeper significance is the fulfilment of Isaiah's sign of the coming salvation.

options.text: That Jesus preferred to heal in private.
options.note: He did take the man aside, but the point is the prophetic sign fulfilled, not a preference for privacy.

options.text: That the man's deafness was caused by his sin.
options.note: The text makes no such claim; the healing displays the dawning age of salvation.

questions: Jesus warned against honouring God with the lips while the heart is far from Him. Where might your worship be more outward form than inward reality?
The Corban rule used religion to dodge a plain duty. Are there ways you use religious activity to avoid the harder obedience God actually asks?
Jesus says defilement comes from within. Which of the sins He lists most needs to be confessed and cleansed in your own heart?
The Syrophoenician woman would not be put off and trusted Jesus for mercy she knew she did not deserve. How does her humble persistence challenge and encourage your own prayers?
The crowds said Jesus does all things well. Where do you need to trust that He is doing all things well, even now, in your life?

translationNotes.note: The BSB does not print a verse 16 in the main text, since the words some manuscripts add here, if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear, are not in the earliest witnesses; the numbering therefore skips from 15 to 17.
The parenthesis thus all foods are clean is Mark's own inspired comment on Jesus' teaching, signalling that the food laws no longer separate; it is confirmed in Acts 10 and Romans 14.
Ephphatha is Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke; Mark preserves the actual word and translates it, be opened, as the deaf ears and bound tongue are freed.
